doc.title: George "Pops" Foster and Mugsy Spanier Interview, 1957-04-21

title: Sitting in with Oliver, baseball and the first record
summary: Mugsy sat in with Oliver's band, gave up baseball for cornet, played Clark Street cabarets and made the Bucktown Five record.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: At Dreamland. How old were you then? About fourteen, thirteen, about fourteen. Did you know him by this time? Oh, yes. I knew him. You were speaking to him? Oh, yes. Sure. Was he nice to you? Very nice. Very nice. He thought it was wonderful that someone could try to play like him. Did you ever get together with him? Oh, yes. I was privileged to be one of the first white persons to sit in with Joe's band. Oh, yeah? Because he wouldn't let you sit in if you couldn't play. He didn't care who you were. Uh-huh. And they had such a good jazz band that they didn't want anyone sitting in there going to spoil the band. Yeah. Joe liked you or he didn't like you. He was a highly sensitive person too. Uh-huh. Did he ever like show you things or, I mean, kind of informally teach you or was it- No, just listening. Just listening. That's all. Absorbing. That's right. And, of course, you know, everyone was coming down to hear Joe, you know. He wasn't very popular, but one of the musicians he was. What were some of the other musicians who after you began to- Well, Brunus and Paul Mraz, Rapolda, Ben Pollack, and El Meshogo, we all used to go down near Joe. Uh-huh. And Steve Brown, a bass player. Uh-huh. We'd all go down, we'd get through working, we'd all go on the south side and stay out there about six, seven, eight o'clock in the morning. And then, you know, Joe, what, uh, I think- What was the name of that cafe across the street from the sunset? Royal Garden? No, Plantation. Plantation? Yeah. And Joe and Plantation, I used to have to go in there and say hello to him. And then Louie was working across the street- At the sunset? At the sunset. And after I'd see Joe, I'd have to go over and say hello to Louie, because Louie, he'd get angry. In the back of bed, so I- In other words, everybody was very friendly with each other at the start. Oh, yes, sure. And I used to, I had a big merman then. I'd open the cutout out about the Indiana Avenue and they'd say here he comes. It sounded like an airplane. I used to take Joe home, I'd get his papers for him. You used to drive him home? Oh, yes. Is that so? He used to hang in a pool room. He was a good pool shooter. Oh, yeah. I forget, I think it was 31st and Indiana, and he'd be in there whenever you wanted Joe in the afternoon, you'd find him in that pool room. You'd be shooting in the pool. Oh, if there was a baseball game, he'd be in the pool room. Yeah. But I remember that, I think Joe used to play at the White Sox ballpark. I'd find a pool and all the best to play out for somebody eating. Because I was going to make a training trip with the Giants, so my mother would let me. And I used to go to the White Sox ballpark and work out out there. And I didn't know who that. Joe was playing in the bleachers out there. And I'd hear this cornet and I'd be pitching and I couldn't concentrate on pitching. I was listening to the musical. So that ended my baseball. Were you playing ball then? Oh, yes, I was playing ball. I pitched for Chicago Furnamon. Oh, yeah? Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. I pitched against Buck Weaver. Oh, yeah? Oh, yeah. You became also professional baseball player. Oh, yeah. My mother would let me make the trip to Florida or wherever the Giants were training then. Oh, for the class? Well, I'd go to school. Uh-huh. I was going to school, playing the cornet too. My sister at school knew I'd be working all night so I'd come in at 9.30 in the morning and I'd go a half a day to school, one day and then a full day the next, catch up on my sleep. Mm-hmm. They were very nice to be the sisters there. Got all my marks so I was all right. What kind of clubs were you playing? Oh, cabarets in those days. You know, this is a four piece band, a five piece band. I was fortunate though, we always had a five piece band. Worked every place on Clark Street, thrown out of more places when I first started to play. I was like, I'm going to go home. So, I sort of licked that. I put on long pants, trying to make myself be older. Because those days when you put on long pants, you were considered a man then. You all right, Pop? Yeah. I don't have my brother's pants, I don't have one bad. That's what I used to do. I'd take my brother's long pants out where they'd just let me in the dreamland. Then one night, Big Brownie used to be the doorman at the peak end there. See? He says, oh, go on upstairs. I'd never been in the peak end. So Joe, I'll be there. I just sat down all over myself with Coca-Cola. I didn't want to go home. When did you start to, when did you make your first record? First record I made was Bucktown Five. First record I ever made. Who was with you? The Bucktown Five? The Bucktown Five. The Lolly Defoe. Mel Stitzel. Marvin Saxby on the guitar. And uh, Die Carey on Trombone myself. I used to have those records. You used to have those records. Good records, too. I don't have them, though. Really? You used to have those records with the rhythm case? When you went to, uh, Myth? Mm-mm. I got a picture there with you. Where?
